title: Landing Day Rehearsal

pages.text:
*The Handbook of Small Truths, Entry 14: Practice is the art of making mistakes where they are cheap.*

The workshop smelled of rust and old grease, a scent that Kess had long ago learned to associate with hope rather than decay. In the center of the dusty floor stood their creation: a full-size manifold mock-up welded from scrap pipe, a tangle of steel that looked less like a radiator joint and more like the skeletal remains of a very aggressive insect. It was ugly, functional, and absolutely critical.

Lio stood before it, encased in the bulky white EVA suit that made him look like an astronaut who had been left in the laundry too long. His helmet was off, resting on a crate, revealing his wavy dark hair pushed back and the faint sheen of sweat on his olive skin. He wore his navy flight-deck jumpsuit underneath, the orange shoulder stripes stark against the white foam of the suit.

"Ready?" asked Chief Voss, who leaned against the wall with his arms crossed, his ginger beard twitching with what might have been amusement or impatience. He held a wrench in one hand, though he hadn't used it in an hour.

"Ready to lose my mind," Lio said. He turned his attention to the valve handle, a simple quarter-turn mechanism that was supposed to be easy. In the suit, it was not easy. The gloves were thick, layered with insulation and abrasion resistance, and they turned his dexterous fingers into clumsy sausages.

Pim stood three meters away, holding a kitchen stopwatch with the solemnity of a race official. "Go," he said, and clicked the button.

Lio gripped the valve. He pulled. The handle resisted. He pulled again, his shoulders hunching, the joints of the suit creaking like the groaning of a ship under heavy load. It was a simple turn, but the friction in the sleeve, combined with the bulk of his hands, made it a feat of strength rather than skill. He grunted, a low sound in his throat, and finally the valve clicked into place.

"Time!" Pim shouted, his voice cracking slightly. "Fourteen seconds."

Voss shook his head slowly. "In the void, you have to do that in under ten. And you have to do it with one hand, because the other will be holding the tether."

Lio removed his gloves, his fingers trembling slightly from the effort. He flexed them, watching the skin tighten and loosen. It was a small thing, a single valve, but in the context of the repair, it was everything. If he couldn't turn a valve, he couldn't seal the leak. And if he couldn't seal the leak, the orchard died.

"I can get faster," Lio said, his voice quiet but firm. He looked at the valve, then at Kess, who was watching from the shadows near the tool bench. "Give me another go."

Kess nodded. She didn't say anything. She didn't need to. She knew the look in his eyes. It was the same look she saw in the mirror when she was trying to graft a stubborn branch. It was the look of someone who refused to accept that the world was harder than they were.
pages.image: Inside a dusty barn with scrap pipe machinery, a tall boy in a bulky white EVA suit struggles to turn a metal valve while a small boy in a red hoodie times him with a stopwatch, an elderly woman with white hair watches nearby, and a bearded man leans against a wall observing.

pages.text:
The first test failed with a hiss that sounded like a deflating balloon left in the heat.

Kess watched the patch sleeve, a clamp-on cylinder of graphite-fiber composite, sit on the mock-up joint. It was elegant in theory, a modern solution to an old problem. In practice, it was leaking coolant at the seam, a fine mist that sprayed across the floor and evaporated before it hit the ground.

"Pressure drop," Voss said, his voice flat. He wiped the mist away with a rag, then wiped his hands on his coverall, leaving a smear of grease on the grey fabric. "It's not holding."

"It should hold," Lio said, stepping forward. He was still in his jumpsuit, having removed the suit for this test. He looked at the joint with the critical eye of an engineer. "The gasket is graphite. It's rated for ten bar."

"Then why is it leaking?" Voss asked.

Kess knelt down, her knees pressing into the cold steel decking. She ran her fingers along the seam of the sleeve. It felt smooth, cold, and dry. But there was a spot, a very small spot, where the metal of the pipe seemed to bite into the gasket. She pulled out her magnifying glass, a small brass-rimmed lens that her mother had given her for spotting pests.

There. A tiny burr, a sliver of metal no wider than a hair, had been left on the pipe when they had cut it for the mock-up. It was a microscopic defect, invisible to the naked eye, but enough to pierce the gasket under pressure.

"Two millimeters," Kess said, pointing to the spot. "A burr. It's piercing the gasket."

Lio looked at the spot, then at Kess. "You can see that?"

"With the lens. And with my hands. I feel the ridge." She handed him the lens. "Lio, can you feel it?"

He leaned in, his eyes narrowing. He ran his finger over the spot. "Yes. It's rough. Like sandpaper."

"Can you fix it?" Voss asked.

Lio looked at his own hands. They were steady, but they were not the hands of someone in a suit. "I can deburr it. But I have to do it blind, or with the lens. And I have to do it without moving the pipe."

"Try it," Voss said. "Take your time."

Lio picked up a small deburring tool, a simple file with a fine edge. He held the lens up to the light, then to the joint. He placed the file against the burr, applying just enough pressure to remove the metal without damaging the pipe. It was delicate work, the kind that required patience and a steady hand. He worked in silence, his breath shallow, his eyes fixed on the tiny sliver of metal.

When he finished, he blew away the metal shavings. He looked up at Kess. "Done."

"Again," Voss said. He began to crank the pressure pump.

The second test failed differently. This time, the leak was not at the seam, but at the clamps. The metal of the clamp had warped slightly, leaving a gap that the gasket couldn't seal.

Kess exhaled slowly, the tension draining from her shoulders. "We're getting closer," she said. "But we're not there yet."

Lio straightened up, wiping his forehead with the back of his hand. "One more time," he said. "I can feel where it's slipping."
pages.image: A close-up of a metal pipe joint with a small leak spraying mist, a girl with a silver streak in her hair points at a tiny burr on the pipe with a small brass magnifying glass, while a boy in a navy suit holds a fine file and watches intently, a bearded man pumps a manual pressure gauge nearby.

pages.text:
The Council Hall smelled of polished wood and cold coffee, a scent that Kess associated with authority and decisions that had gone stale in the drawer. She carried a tray of three perfect cups, the steam rising in thin, lazy curls that danced in the recycled air. Pim walked beside her, his sneakers pulsing a soft green rhythm with each step, his eyes wide with a mixture of awe and the particular terror of being twelve in a room full of adults.

They had visited four councilors so far. Two had been sympathetic, one indifferent, and the fourth, Ferris Quill, had been a wall of skepticism so dense it required a drill.

Quill sat in his office, a narrow room lined with shelves of data crystals. He was a tall man with sharp features and sleek white hair. He did not stand when they entered. He did not smile. He simply looked at the tea, then at Kess, and raised one eyebrow.

"You brought me tea," he said. It was not a question.

"Yes, Councilor," Kess replied. "I hope it's not too strong."

"I don't drink tea," Quill said. He looked at the cup, then at the one-page summary Kess had placed on his desk. "You brought me a document. A summary of numbers I have already read."

"I brought you the opportunity to check them," Kess said. She placed a magnifying glass on the desk, next to the paper. "Every figure is sourced. Every calculation is shown. I invite you to check every single one. If you find an error, I will withdraw my petition."

Quill looked at the magnifying glass, then at Kess. His eyes were hard, but there was a flicker of something else there. Respect, perhaps. Or curiosity. He picked up the glass and held it over the first line of the summary.

He read the first number. He read the second. He read the third. His eyebrows, which had been flat and skeptical, began to rise. Slowly, incrementally, they climbed. He moved to the second paragraph. His eyebrows climbed higher. He moved to the third.

Kess watched him, her hands resting on the edge of the desk. She did not speak. She did not need to. The numbers were the truth, and the truth did not need a voice.

Quill set the magnifying glass down. He looked at Kess, and for the first time, his expression softened. It was not a smile, but it was a relaxation. A letting go.

"I withdraw one objection," he said.

Pim, who had been standing silently in the corner, let out a small, sharp gasp. Kess felt a warmth spread through her chest, a feeling that was not quite joy, but close to it.

"Thank you, Councilor," she said.

Quill picked up the tea. He sniffed it. "It is not too strong," he said. "It is acceptable."
pages.image: In a dim office with shelves of data crystals, a tall man with iron-colored hair looks up from a document with his eyebrows raised in surprise, holding a magnifying glass, while a girl with a silver streak in her hair stands calmly with a tray of tea, and a small boy in a red hoodie watches from the corner.

pages.text:
Councilor Hale's office sat in a low amber half-light, the kind that made the shadows feel less like darkness and more like a held breath. The room was cramped, cluttered with stacks of paper and small potted herbs that looked as though they were negotiating for their own survival against the artificial air. Hale sat behind her desk, her silver-streaked auburn hair pulled back in a neat bun, her charcoal tunic crisp against the clutter.

Kess sat opposite, hands clasped in her lap. Pim had been dismissed with a gentle wave, leaving with a look of profound disappointment that suggested he was already drafting a list of grievances.

"You have been busy," Hale said. Her voice was soft, carrying the specific weariness of someone who has been carrying heavy things for a long time. "Ferris Quill is not a man who gives up his objections lightly."

"He checks the numbers," Kess said. "He likes to be right."

Hale smiled, a thin, sad expression. "He is right about many things. But he is wrong about this." She leaned forward, elbows on the desk. "Kess, have you read the confidential reports? The ones from the last ten years?"

Kess nodded. She had read them all, with Pim, with Lio, with Voss. She had read them with her own eyes, and she had seen the truth.

"They are bad," Kess said.

"They are very bad," Hale said. "And I have hated Directive Nine for years. I have hated it because it keeps me in the dark. I have hated it because it makes me a liar by default. I have feared the panic, yes. I have feared that the people of this ship would lose hope. But I have feared something else more."

"What?" Kess asked.

"The truth," Hale said. "I have feared that the truth is not enough. That even if we fix the leak, we will not be able to fix the fear. That the ship is sick, and we are only treating the symptoms."

Kess looked at Hale. She saw the exhaustion in the Councilor's eyes, the quiet burden of responsibility that sat on her shoulders like a heavy coat. She thought of the orchard, the trees, the apples. She thought of the future, the grandchildren, the long voyage.

"I am certain of the numbers," Kess said. "But I am not certain of the outcome. I am not certain that we can fix the ship. I am not certain that we can save the orchard. But I am certain that we must try. And I am certain that we must tell the truth."

Hale looked at her for a long moment. Then she nodded.

"That is the correct answer," she said. "Not the perfect answer. Not the easy answer. But the correct one."

Kess felt a sense of relief, a lightening of the air in the room. It was not a victory, not yet. But it was a step. A small, honest step.

"Thank you, Councilor," Kess said.

Hale waved her hand. "Go. You have work to do. And Kess?"

"Yes?"

"Bring me another cup of tea. Next time."

pages.text:
The workshop hummed with the low, constant thrum of the pressure pump, a sound Kess had learned to read like the wind in the branches. The mock-up joint sat on the workbench under the bare bulbs, the patch sleeve seated and the clamps tightened with a meticulous precision that held the room’s tension in a single, taut thread. Voss stood beside the gauge, his face grim, watching the needle hold steady at two bar.

"Two bar," he said, his voice flat. "It holds."

Kess nodded, though her stomach tightened with a dull ache. Two bar was the pressure of the orchard’s internal cooling loop, safe and familiar, but the radiator wing ran at six. She could feel the discrepancy in her teeth, the gap between what they had and what they needed.

"We need a safety margin," Voss said, not looking up from the gauge. "Standard procedure is twenty percent. That means we need to pass a test at eight bar."

Kess did the arithmetic in her head, her mind racing over the numbers like a hand over rough bark. Eight bar. The patch had failed at five. They had not pushed it to the limit, nor had they found the breaking point, only the point where it gave up.

"We have eight days," she said, her voice steady despite the tremor in her hands. "And a patch that fails at five."

Lio, who had been leaning against the tool bench with his arms crossed, straightened up. His face was pale, his eyes wide with the specific apprehension of someone who knows the math but cannot see the way out. "We can't test it at eight in here," he said. "If it blows, the shrapnel will take the gauges, and if it fails, we have no time to fix it."

"We have no time to fail," Voss said, finally turning to face Kess. "It is your call. You understand the system. You know the ship."

Kess looked at the mock-up, then at the gauge, and finally at her friends, their faces reflecting the same tenuous hope and the same heavy burden. She thought of the trees, the apples, the long voyage ahead, and the simple, honest truth that a future is something people maintain.

"We don't test it at eight," she said, her voice finding a new, quiet strength. "We make it stronger. We find a way to make it hold at eight. And then we test it at ten."

Voss raised an eyebrow, his thick ginger beard twitching. "Ten?"

"Yes," Kess said. "If it holds at ten, it will hold at eight. And if it holds at eight, we are safe."

It was a risk, a huge and terrifying one, but it was the only way. It was the way of the engineer, the way of the gardener, the way of making the impossible possible, one small, honest step at a time.

"Let's get to work," Kess said.
